# Use AI to widen the search, not choose the research bet

For topic selection, the most defensible role for AI is to enlarge and organize the possibility space. A model can propose alternative formulations, connect a problem to adjacent literatures, identify assumptions, and generate tests that might quickly eliminate weak directions. It should not decide which question deserves several years of a researcher’s attention. That decision combines novelty, feasibility, scholarly value, and personal conviction—judgments that a fluent ranking of candidate topics cannot settle. This is the publication’s inference from the evidence, not a demonstrated universal rule. <!-- claim:01-c5 -->

The strongest quantitative evidence comes from a narrower setting. On 36 combinatorial-optimization problems, the LACE framework reported an average score of 0.945, versus 0.870 for the strongest LLM-based comparator and 0.571 for direct prompting. These are reported results from the framework’s authors, who evaluated methods using a shared model backbone. LACE did not simply ask a model for a finished algorithm: it specified a verified problem contract, supplied tools, decomposed the task, and iteratively selected complementary heuristics. The comparison suggests that structure and testing can matter more than one-shot model output. <!-- claim:01-c1 -->

That result offers a useful analogy for topic discovery. Instead of asking, “What should my dissertation be about?”, a student could define constraints such as available data, acceptable computational cost, relevant theory, and the kind of contribution sought. The model could then generate competing problem statements, search for nearby work, and propose falsification tests. A Nature commentary describes a related approach to evidence exploration: staged search, an evolving evidence graph, and a revisable checklist updated as new findings arrive. This is the commentary authors’ proposed model of investigation, not proof that such a workflow identifies important research questions. <!-- claim:01-c3 -->

The human role begins well before final approval. An MIT expert argues that routine calculations, coding, failed approaches, and small discoveries help graduate students acquire intuition; delegating them can remove formative experiences even while enabling more ambitious projects. On this view, problem formulation and auditing are part of the education, not merely overhead to automate away. For an AI or operations-research student, repeatedly discovering why an apparently attractive formulation is ill-posed may build exactly the judgment needed to recognize a worthwhile topic later. This is a source claim about graduate training, rather than a controlled estimate of learning loss. <!-- claim:01-c2 -->

Topic choice also reflects institutional incentives. In a Latent Space interview, Alex Zhang attributes some of academia’s distinctiveness to pursuing problems that industry labs are not currently optimizing for, while warning that graduate students may gravitate toward work that looks attractive to those labs. That is practitioner testimony, not controlled evidence, and the technology-focused publisher benefits from interest in agent systems. Still, it identifies a real failure mode: an AI search tool trained on visible, popular work may make crowded benchmarks look more promising precisely because they are easier to retrieve and summarize. <!-- claim:01-c4 -->

A workable division of labor follows. Let the model generate several research bets, including unfashionable or adversarial alternatives, but require an evidence record for each: closest prior work, unresolved contradiction, required resources, decisive experiment, and conditions under which the idea is no longer novel. The student should inspect the cited papers, test computational assumptions, and write the final rationale in terms they can defend. AI can compress the search, but the researcher must decide which uncertainties are scientifically productive rather than merely inconvenient. <!-- claim:01-c3 --><!-- claim:01-c5 -->

There is an important counterargument. Human control does not guarantee originality: advisers and students can be conservative, status-driven, or unaware of adjacent fields. Nor does LACE establish that constrained AI search improves dissertation selection; its benchmark concerns algorithm construction, uses one shared model backbone, and includes new problems designed by its authors. Evidence graphs improve traceability without proving that retrieved evidence is correct or that a topic matters. The lesson is therefore conditional: AI-assisted exploration is valuable when it makes alternatives and assumptions inspectable, not when its ranked answer substitutes for judgment. <!-- claim:01-c1 --><!-- claim:01-c3 --><!-- claim:01-c5 -->

The cost of ignoring that distinction is that generation scales faster than verification. Retraction Watch reported a case in which a sign error invalidated one mathematical argument and constructions used by two dependent manuscripts. That episode does not estimate the general error rate of AI-assisted research, but it shows how dependencies can propagate a mistake across polished outputs. Topic discovery should exploit scale while ideas are still cheap to discard; commitment should wait for human scrutiny of novelty, feasibility, and evidence. <!-- claim:01-c5 -->

# Replace one-shot drafting with a verified research pipeline

The defensible unit of AI assistance is a pipeline, not a passage. A generated paragraph may be elegant while concealing a broken citation, an untested computation, or a dependency on an earlier error. A research pipeline instead exposes inputs, transformations, tools, tests, and revisions. Across the supplied sources, the publication’s inference is that efficiency and rigor are compatible when verification occurs during generation rather than after the prose has acquired an undeserved appearance of completion. <!-- claim:02-c5 -->

LACE provides quantitative evidence for this principle in algorithm design. Its modular framework defined input and output schemas, a tool library, a verified problem contract, and an iterative process for generating and selecting heuristics. The authors reported a Valid Rate of 0.944; none of the compared LLM-based baselines exceeded 0.611. This is a reported benchmark result, not evidence about prose drafting directly. It nevertheless shows that decomposing work and checking feasibility can produce far more reliable outputs than asking the same class of model to solve the whole task in one pass. <!-- claim:02-c1 -->

For writing, the analogous pipeline begins with claims rather than sentences. A draft section should be treated as a collection of propositions linked to primary sources, computations, or clearly labeled interpretation. The model can propose an outline, identify missing transitions, or produce alternative explanations. Before those suggestions enter the manuscript, externally checkable claims should be compared with the underlying papers, and numerical results should be reproduced from code or data. Polishing comes after the claim-to-evidence structure survives inspection. This workflow is an inference from evidence across several domains, not a validated recipe with a measured effect size. <!-- claim:02-c5 -->

The danger of postponing verification appears in a Retraction Watch report about OpenAI’s mass release of mathematics manuscripts. According to the report, OpenAI withdrew three manuscripts after a sign error invalidated an argument in one and constructions used by two dependent papers. The company also reported revisions to 14 other manuscripts. These are reported facts about a particular release, not an estimated base rate for AI-generated mathematics. Their importance lies in the dependency structure: one local error can contaminate several downstream results when generation proceeds faster than validation. <!-- claim:02-c2 -->

Citation checking is a simpler instance of the same problem. In a SciSpace video, a journal and grant reviewer advises researchers to test every AI-supplied DOI and confirm that it resolves to the intended work. This is practitioner guidance rather than controlled evidence, and SciSpace sells research software. Even so, the test is concrete and falsifiable. A DOI that resolves is not sufficient—the destination must have the claimed authors, result, and relevance—but failure at this first check immediately exposes a defective citation. <!-- claim:02-c3 -->

Provenance should cover more than the bibliography. In a Latent Space interview, representatives of Periodic Labs say their system records conversations, intuitions, laboratory actions, computations, and code so models can learn from the process of science rather than only final outputs. This is the company’s description of its practice, not independent validation of its platform. The useful principle is lineage: when a conclusion changes, a researcher should be able to locate the affected evidence, analysis, and prose instead of rereading a polished manuscript as though it were the complete history of the work. <!-- claim:02-c4 -->

For an AI or operations-research project, this might mean maintaining a claim ledger beside the manuscript. Each consequential statement points to a source location, an experiment identifier, or an executable test; model-generated alternatives remain labeled until accepted; and dependent claims are rechecked after any correction. This is not clerical maximalism. It lets researchers revise locally, identify which conclusions survive a failed assumption, and use models for rapid iteration without confusing throughput with confidence. <!-- claim:02-c4 --><!-- claim:02-c5 -->

The counterargument is cost. Full formal verification is unavailable for much empirical work, and checking every minor sentence can consume the time AI was meant to save. Relevance, novelty, and explanatory value also resist mechanical tests. LACE’s success on combinatorial optimization does not show that every scholarly judgment can be encoded as a contract. A sensible pipeline therefore allocates scrutiny according to consequence: central claims, citations, computations, and dependencies receive explicit checks, while stylistic suggestions receive lighter review. <!-- claim:02-c1 --><!-- claim:02-c5 -->

This leaves the researcher with more responsibility, not less. AI can accelerate candidate generation, repair, and revision, but a polished output is only an interface. Confidence should come from the visible chain beneath it: evidence inspected, computations rerun, references resolved, failures retained, and revisions propagated. The efficiency gain is not avoiding scrutiny; it is arranging the work so that scrutiny happens before errors become structural. <!-- claim:02-c2 --><!-- claim:02-c5 -->

# Authorship after AI: responsibility cannot be delegated

AI complicates the evidence of authorship without changing its central obligation. Researchers may delegate searches, candidate proofs, code drafts, summaries, and editorial revisions. They cannot delegate responsibility for what the paper asks readers to believe. The relevant standard is therefore not how many sentences the researcher typed, but whether they can trace, reproduce, explain, and defend the work—and correct or withdraw it when support fails. This is the publication’s inference from the combined evidence. <!-- claim:03-c5 -->

Fluent reasoning text is a particularly weak substitute for that responsibility. The Nature perspective “Characterizing the role of reasoning tokens in large language models as state over tokens” argues that a model’s displayed reasoning can be a plausible derivation of an answer without faithfully describing the process that produced it. This is the authors’ conceptual and evidence-based claim, not proof that every displayed derivation is false or useless. Such text may still help a researcher inspect individual steps, but it should not be treated as a model audit log. <!-- claim:03-c1 -->

That distinction matters whenever an author says the model “reasoned” its way to a result. A derivation can be mathematically checkable even if it is not a faithful causal account of the system. Conversely, a convincing narrative can contain a hidden gap. The author must therefore validate the derivation on its own terms—by proof checking, execution, replication, or comparison with sources—rather than relying on the apparent transparency of the generated rationale. The broader inference is that plausibility should trigger inspection, not calibrated trust by itself. <!-- claim:03-c1 --><!-- claim:03-c5 -->

MIT’s Alexander Rakhlin frames academic evaluation around identifiable contribution and intellectual responsibility, including when substantial parts of the work were performed by AI. That is a source claim about how universities should assess researchers. It shifts disclosure away from a crude word-count model. A student might type little yet make the decisive contribution by formulating the problem, rejecting invalid approaches, designing the evaluation, and defending the conclusion. Another might edit every generated sentence while remaining unable to explain the assumptions or reproduce the result. <!-- claim:03-c2 -->

The practical test is control over evidence and decisions. An author should know which claims came from which sources, which computations were executed, which model suggestions were rejected, and what changed after a failed experiment. Where applicable policies require disclosure, material AI assistance should be reported accurately. The supplied evidence does not establish a universal disclosure threshold, so researchers must consult the relevant journal, conference, institution, and funder rather than infer a single rule from general principles. <!-- claim:03-c2 --><!-- claim:03-c5 -->

The consequences of weak control are illustrated by Retraction Watch’s report on OpenAI’s release of mathematics manuscripts. An OpenAI spokesperson said roughly half of the results were released unconfirmed; the report followed withdrawals and revisions prompted by errors. This is a reported statement about one unusually large release, not evidence that half of AI-assisted research generally fails. It nevertheless shows why scale changes the burden of responsibility: when hundreds of outputs and their dependencies appear at once, rapid correction does not replace verification before release. <!-- claim:03-c3 -->

A reviewer speaking in a SciSpace video offers a complementary standard: AI should help produce good research, not merely more research. This is practitioner guidance, and the publisher has a commercial interest in AI-mediated research workflows. Its value is normative rather than statistical. For a PhD student, increased volume is worthwhile only if it expands tested alternatives, improves clarity, or strengthens evidence. More drafts, citations, and candidate theorems are liabilities when the author cannot inspect them at the rate they are produced. <!-- claim:03-c4 -->

Process lineage offers one way to make responsibility visible. Periodic Labs says it records conversations, intuitions, laboratory actions, computations, and code so that models learn from the process rather than only the final product. That is a company account, not independent proof of effectiveness. Adapted cautiously, the idea supports an authorship record containing claim-to-source links, experiment versions, decision notes, and the reasons for accepting or rejecting model output. Such a record need not be public in full to help an author answer a reviewer or investigate an error. <!-- claim:03-c5 -->

There are limits. Human authorship has never guaranteed correctness, and requiring exhaustive logs can expose confidential data, peer-review material, security-sensitive prompts, or proprietary methods. A displayed derivation can still be useful even if it is not a faithful account of model internals. The right response is proportionate auditability: preserve enough lineage to substantiate important claims and contributions while respecting privacy and legal constraints. Responsibility is not equivalent to indiscriminate surveillance of the research process. <!-- claim:03-c1 --><!-- claim:03-c5 -->

Authorship after AI is thus less about guarding the keyboard than owning the epistemic chain. Researchers should be able to say what the system contributed, what they themselves decided, how each important claim was tested, and what evidence would change their conclusion. If they cannot, disclosure alone does not cure the problem. If they can, substantial AI assistance need not erase authorship—but it does make the author’s burden of verification and explanation more explicit. <!-- claim:03-c2 --><!-- claim:03-c5 -->
